extracted.intended_audience: early-career mathematics instructors (graduate students, postdocs, junior faculty) and those who mentor them
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative principles for teaching undergraduate (and early-career) mathematics courses, with emphasis on student engagement, pedagogy choice, and inclusive support structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the material
rubrics_metrics.description: I have a body of material that I want them to learn. My job is to get as much of it across to them as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the obvious primary goal: deliver core content (e.g., partial derivatives and multiple integrals in multivariable calculus; proof-writing in a first proofs class; homotopy and homology in algebraic topology). Teaching the material certainly is and should be a goal of every course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impart a love of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: We want to impart a love of mathematics. We want to get across the power and beauty of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond content mastery, aim to excite students about the subject so they continue taking courses and potentially pursue lifelong mathematical study. Success here leads to greater long-term learning than any single course’s content alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey enthusiasm (authentically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveying enthusiasm and excitement for the material: varying voice pitch, using hand gestures, trying to exude enthusiasm and connect with the audience through body language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ceci’s experiment—after training to show more enthusiasm his mean enthusiasm score rose from 2.14 to 4.21 and many course-survey metrics increased (knowledgeable 3.61→4.05, accessibility 2.99→4.06, organization 3.18→4.09, perceived learning 2.93→4.05), though exam performance was nearly identical. Enthusiasm increases engagement and students’ experience; avoid forced/inauthentic enthusiasm (students can tell and it backfires).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-rely on student course surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Student course survey data is easily influenced by factors that do not translate into better learning, and therefore colleges should not use this kind of data in their decision-making processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceci & Williams conclude that minor changes in teaching style substantially impact survey scores without corresponding learning gains, so survey scores are imperfect measures of instructional effectiveness—use them cautiously, and not as sole evidence for tenure or promotion decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate teaching by longer-term student engagement/outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether students are more likely to take follow-up courses or continue studies in the field (longer-term indicators of teaching success).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate survey or exam scores may miss benefits such as increased likelihood of continuing in the subject; collect or consider data on subsequent course enrollment and sustained interest as complementary measures of teaching effectiveness (Ceci study lacked such follow-up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with and personalize teaching style
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no one correct method for teaching mathematics; it all depends on who you are and who the students are. Figure out what works for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try different approaches (lecture, flipped classroom, active learning, inquiry-based learning). Example workshop exercise: three-minute presentations with random presentation-role prompts (e.g., 'You are in a Broadway show', 'You HATE this math', 'You’re a used car salesperson', 'You just won the Fields Medal') to explore latitude in style. Use experimentation to discover an authentic, effective style rather than adopting a prescribed 'professorial demeanor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be organized and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Well organized and clear presentation is a hallmark of successful teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization and clarity are necessary components of effective lectures (award-winning instructors are often clear and organized). Coupling clarity with visible enjoyment of the material amplifies student receptivity, but clarity itself is essential even without theatricality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adopting a forced persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not restrict yourself to a particular 'professorial demeanor' or put on an inauthentic persona in the classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let your natural personality show; forcing a manner can look unnatural and reduce effectiveness. The goal is authenticity—students detect forced behavior and it can undermine rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design help resources to avoid reinforcing isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that common support structures (e.g., evening TA help sessions) can make some students feel isolated if they arrive alone and see established groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how normal resource designs can unintentionally signal belonging to some students and exclusion to others. Use this awareness to redesign supports so students who come alone are not stigmatized or left without access to help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide on-demand individual tutoring with low stigma
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement on-demand individual tutoring sessions that students can sign up for without questions, to make it easier to get help without going through the instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implementation: TAs offering individual tutoring coordinate with instructor to set sensible times, create appointment slots (e.g., shared Google calendar) and allow students to sign up anonymously or without explanation. This reduces intimidation and stigma compared to only group help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train TAs about inclusion dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure TAs are aware of dynamics that can harm students’ sense of belonging (e.g., established working groups monopolizing TA attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department-level action: educate TAs about inclusive practices, encourage scheduling of individual sessions, and instruct TAs to be mindful of who is being left out during help sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about pedagogical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit with students about the pedagogical reasons behind course activities (for example, telling students that group work is intended to help them meet one another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency reduces student anxiety, clarifies instructor intent, and signals that course design choices are purposeful—this supports inclusion and helps students understand how activities serve their learning and belonging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to students and use their feedback to change practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage with students (e.g., structured conversations, breakout groups, written prompts) to learn what makes them feel unwelcome or supported, and change practices accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a campus-day conference collected student responses on Post-its and led the author to implement department and course-level changes (on-demand tutoring, TA training, transparency). Regular solicitation of student perspectives reveals hidden harms and actionable fixes.
